Environmental factors have been identified as significant contributors to primary systemic vasculitis, particularly in cases where there is an association with farming, silica, solvents, and allergy. These studies suggest that exposure to certain environmental substances may trigger or exacerbate the condition. For example, a significant association between farming and primary systemic vasculitis has been found, indicating a possible link between farming and PSV (primary systemic vasculitis). Additionally, results have also supported previously reported associations with silica, solvents, and allergy.

Furthermore, detailed analysis of sputum and systemic inflammation in asthma phenotypes suggests that eosinophilic inflammation is present across all categories of asthma, and that paucigranulocytic asthma may be seen as a low-grade inflammatory disease. This finding indicates that environmental factors may play a role in modulating the inflammatory process in asthma.

Regarding primary sleeve gastrectomy for morbid obesity, research has identified risk factors that increase the rate of staple line leakage, including modifiable factors such as lifestyle and adherence to postoperative care protocols. These studies suggest that modifiable risk factors can be used to define high-risk patients and offer targeted interventions to reduce serious complications.

Finally, research on atrial fibrillation suggests that a "second hit," such as an environmental factor like hypertension, may contribute to the manifestation of primary systemic vasculitis. This model would also account for the age-related increase in AF development.

In conclusion, environmental factors appear to be important in primary systemic vasculitis, particularly in cases where there is an association with farming, silica, solvents, and allergy. Further research is needed to fully understand the role of environmental factors in this condition and to develop effective prevention and treatment strategies.
